title: A mixed brainteaser set
objectives: Solve an unlabelled set of brainteasers in interview order at a stated pace.

screens.title: Puzzle 1
screens.prose: Mixed set, about two minutes a puzzle, as an interview allows. Time yourself and say the argument aloud before you answer. A drawer holds socks in 5 colours, many of each. You pick in the dark.

state.caption: Five colours, many socks of each.

screens.question: How many socks must you take to be sure of a matching pair?

hints.text: What is the worst luck you can have?
Five socks can all differ.
The sixth must match one.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Picture the worst case first.

byKey.five: Five socks can be one of each colour, with no pair.
byKey.ten: Ten guarantees two pairs. One pair needs only six.

explain.text: The worst case is one sock of each colour, five in all. The sixth sock must repeat a colour. Principle: more objects than boxes forces a repeat.

screens.title: Puzzle 2
screens.prose: About two minutes; say it aloud first. Thirteen coins lie heads up. A move turns over exactly four of them, any four.
screens.question: Can moves ever leave all thirteen tails up?

options.why: Four moves turn sixteen coins, but each move changes the heads by an even number.

options.text: Yes, if some coins are turned back
options.why: Turning a coin back still moves the heads by an even amount.

hints.text: What does one move do to the number of heads?
It changes by 4, 2, 0, −2 or −4.
Thirteen is odd, and 0 is even.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Track the parity of the heads.

byKey.four: Each move changes the heads by an even number, so they stay odd.
byKey.back: Every move changes the heads by 4, 2, 0, −2 or −4, so they stay odd.

explain.text: A move changes the heads by 4, 2, 0, −2 or −4, so the heads stay odd. All tails needs 0 heads, which is even. Principle: look for a quantity no move changes.

screens.title: Puzzle 3
screens.prose: About two minutes; say it aloud first. Before you solve the next puzzle, choose a method. Thirty coins look alike, but one is lighter. You have a balance scale.
screens.question: Which method fits?

options.text: Split into three groups and count outcomes

options.why: A weighing has three outcomes: left, right or level. Halving uses only two.
Colouring proves something impossible. Here you need a search.
Backward induction suits games with turns. A weighing is a search.

hints.text: How many outcomes does one weighing have?
Three: left down, right down, or level.
Use all three by weighing a third against a third.

feedback.correct: Three groups: each weighing has three outcomes.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count a weighing's outcomes.

byKey.halve: Halving ignores the level outcome, which also tells you something.
byKey.colour: Colouring rules things out. Here you must find a coin.
byKey.back: There are no turns to work back from. This is a search.

explain.text: A weighing ends left down, right down or level: three outcomes. So split into three groups and keep the group the scale points to. Principle: count outcomes against cases.

screens.title: Puzzle 4
screens.prose: About two minutes; say it aloud first. Thirty coins look alike, but one is lighter. You have a balance scale.
screens.question: What is the fewest weighings that always finds the light coin?

hints.text: Each weighing at most divides the cases by 3.
Three weighings separate at most $3^3 = 27$ coins.
30 is more than 27, and $3^4 = 81$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare 30 with powers of 3.

byKey.three: Three weighings give $3^3 = 27$ outcomes, fewer than 30 coins.
byKey.halve: 5 comes from halving. A weighing has three outcomes, so 4 suffice.

explain.text: Three weighings have $3^3 = 27$ outcomes, too few for 30 coins. Four have 81, and splitting 10, 10, 10 then 4, 3, 3 works. Principle: $27 < 30 \le 81$, so 4.

screens.title: Puzzle 5
screens.prose: About two minutes; say it aloud first. A 7 × 7 board loses the square next to one corner. Dominoes each cover two neighbouring squares.

state.caption: The square next to the top-left corner is removed.

screens.question: Can 24 dominoes cover the 48 squares that are left?

options.why: Even area is needed but not enough. A domino covers one square of each colour.

options.text: Yes, if you start from the far corner
options.why: No order of placing helps. The colour counts are 25 and 23.

hints.text: Colour the board like a chessboard.
The corners are dark. Count each colour after the removal.
Dark 25, light 23. A domino covers one of each.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the two colours.

byKey.yes: Each domino covers one dark and one light square. 25 dark and 23 light cannot pair up.
byKey.start: Where you start does not change the colour counts, 25 and 23.

explain.text: The full board has 25 dark and 24 light squares, and the removed square is light. That leaves 25 against 23, but dominoes cover them one for one. Principle: colour so every piece covers a fixed mix.

screens.title: Puzzle 6
screens.prose: About two minutes; say it aloud first. Choose a method for the next puzzle. Pirates of fixed rank vote on how to share gold, and a rejected proposer goes overboard.
screens.question: Which method fits?

options.text: Split into three groups and count outcomes
options.why: That is for weighings. Here each pirate's choice depends on what happens next.
Colouring proves impossibility. Here you need a best proposal.
Halving ignores the votes. Each vote depends on the later rounds.

hints.text: What happens if only one or two pirates are left?
Solve the smallest crew first.
Each crew size uses the answer for one fewer pirate.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what each pirate expects if the vote fails.

byKey.three: Weighings split cases. Pirates vote by comparing with the next round.
byKey.colour: Nothing here is impossible. You need the proposal that passes.
byKey.halve: The votes, not the gold, drive this puzzle.

explain.text: Each pirate votes by comparing an offer with what the next round would give. So solve the smallest crew and build up. Principle: work back from the end.

screens.title: Puzzle 7
screens.prose: About two minutes; say it aloud first. Pirates A, B and C, ranked in that order, share 50 coins. A proposes and all vote, A included. At least half yes passes; otherwise A goes overboard and B proposes. Each wants to live, then coins, then to see others go.
screens.question: How many coins does A keep?

hints.text: With two pirates left, what does B propose?
B keeps all 50; his own vote is half. C would get 0.
A needs one more vote. C takes 1 coin over 0.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Solve the two-pirate case first.

byKey.all: A's vote alone is one of three, less than half. A must buy one vote.
byKey.equal: An equal split overpays. C votes yes for a single coin.
byKey.half: A needs only one vote, and C's costs 1 coin.

explain.text: With two pirates, B keeps all 50, so C would get 0. A buys C's vote with 1 coin and keeps 49. Principle: each pirate compares the offer with the next round.

screens.title: Puzzle 8
screens.prose: About two minutes; say it aloud first. Fifteen people stand in a line, each in a red or blue hat. Each sees every hat in front, not their own. From the back, each says one colour aloud. They agree a plan first.

containers.label: Back of the line on the left

screens.question: How many can be sure to be right?

hints.text: The back person sees 14 hats. What can one word tell the rest?
Say blue if the number of red hats seen is even.
Everyone else hears that parity and every later answer.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Let the back person announce a parity.

byKey.all: The back person sees no clue to their own hat, so nobody can promise them.
byKey.half: Pairing up wastes half the calls. One parity bit serves everyone.

explain.text: The back person announces the parity of the red hats ahead. Each next person compares it with what they see and hear, and deduces their own. Principle: one parity bit can carry everyone's answer.

screens.title: Puzzle 9
screens.prose: About two minutes; say it aloud first. Four people cross a bridge at night with one torch. At most two cross at once, at the slower one's pace. They take 1, 2, 6 and 9 minutes.
screens.question: What is the shortest total time, in minutes?

hints.text: Should the two slowest cross together?
Send 1 and 2, return 1, send 6 and 9, return 2.
Then 1 and 2 cross again.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Let the two slowest cross together.

byKey.escort: Having 1 escort everyone gives $2 + 1 + 6 + 1 + 9 = 19$. Pairing 6 with 9 saves time.
byKey.sum: Adding every time ignores the returns and the pairing. Plan the trips.

explain.text: Send 1 and 2, return 1, send 6 and 9, return 2, send 1 and 2. That takes $2 + 1 + 9 + 2 + 2 = 16$ minutes. Principle: let the two slowest share one trip.

screens.title: Puzzle 10
screens.prose: About two minutes; say it aloud first. You cycle to a market at 30 km/h and back by the same road at 60 km/h.
screens.question: What is your average speed for the round trip?

options.why: You averaged the speeds. The slow leg takes twice as long, so it weighs more.
You added the speeds. An average lies between them.

hints.text: Pick a distance, say 60 km each way.
Out takes 2 hours, back takes 1.
120 km in 3 hours.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide total distance by total time.

byKey.45: 45 is the plain mean. You spend 2 hours slow and only 1 fast.
byKey.90: The average cannot exceed the faster speed.

explain.text: Take 60 km each way: 2 hours out and 1 back, so 120 km in 3 hours. That is 40 km/h, the harmonic mean $\tfrac{2 \cdot 30 \cdot 60}{90}$. Principle: over equal distances, add the times.

screens.title: Puzzle 11
screens.prose: About two minutes; say it aloud first. A train leaves at 2 p.m. for a city 300 km away.
screens.question: When does it arrive?

options.text: Ask for its speed: the time cannot be found without it

options.why: You assumed a speed. An interviewer wants to hear you ask for it.
You assumed a speed. The question gives none.

hints.text: What do you need besides the distance?
Time is distance over speed.
No speed is given.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check what the question gives you.

byKey.five: 100 km/h is your guess, not a fact of the puzzle. Ask.
byKey.seven: 60 km/h is your guess, not a fact of the puzzle. Ask.

explain.text: Arrival needs distance over speed, and no speed is given. Asking is the right answer, not a failure. Principle: name the missing fact before you compute.

screens.title: Puzzle 12
screens.prose: Follow-up, as a mock first round. The interviewer adds a fifth person to puzzle 9, who takes 12 minutes. The times are 1, 2, 6, 9 and 12, under the same rules.
screens.question: What is the shortest total time now, in minutes?

hints.text: Ferry the two slowest, 9 and 12, together.
1 and 2 cross, 1 back, 9 and 12 cross, 2 back: 17 minutes.
Then 1, 2 and 6 remain: 9 more minutes.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Send the two slowest together with the shuttle.

byKey.escort: Having 1 escort everyone gives 32. The shuttle saves time on the slow pair.
byKey.wrongpair: Pairing 6 with 9 leaves 12 to cross with an escort. Pair 9 with 12.

explain.text: The shuttle takes 9 and 12 over in $2 + 1 + 12 + 2 = 17$ minutes. Then 1 and 6 cross, 1 returns and 1 and 2 cross: $6 + 1 + 2 = 9$. The total is 26, and a search over every plan confirms it.

ideas: Name the family first: invariant, colouring, pigeonhole, weighing, induction, parity code or rate.
Say the method aloud before any arithmetic, then check the smallest case.
When a fact is missing, ask for it: that is part of the answer.

formula.name: Outcomes against cases
formula.note: Weighings for one light coin, and the average speed there and back.

summary.trap: Out at 30 km/h and back at 60 averages 40, not 45.

quiz.prose: Twenty prisoners each open 10 of 20 boxes, following the cycle from their own number. All must find their own number.
quiz.question: What is the chance they all succeed? Give four decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. They fail only when a cycle is longer than 10.

byKey.half: 1/2 is one prisoner's chance alone. The cycle strategy links their fates.
byKey.limit: $1 - \ln 2 = 0.3069$ is the limit for large crowds. With 20 it is a little higher.

explain.text: They fail exactly when some cycle is longer than 10, which has chance $\tfrac{1}{11} + \cdots + \tfrac{1}{20}$. So the chance of success is $1 - 0.6688 = 0.3312$. Principle: a cycle of length $k > n/2$ has chance $1/k$.

quiz.prose: You have two eggs and a 120-floor building. Find the highest safe floor in the fewest drops, worst case.
quiz.question: How many drops do you need?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the smallest $t$ with $t(t+1)/2 \ge 120$.

byKey.root: $\sqrt{120}$ is about 11, but the gaps must shrink by one each drop.

explain.text: With $t$ drops the first egg starts at floor $t$, then gaps of $t - 1$, $t - 2$ and so on. That covers $t(t+1)/2$ floors, and $15 \cdot 16/2 = 120$. Principle: shrink each gap by one.

quiz.question: What is the angle between the hands, in degrees?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $|30h - 5.5m|$, then take the smaller angle.

byKey.reflex: 205 is the long way round. Take $360 - 205$.
byKey.stuck: You left the hour hand on the 4. By 4:50 it is 25° on.

explain.text: $|30 \cdot 4 - 5.5 \cdot 50| = |120 - 275| = 155$. That is under 180, so it is the angle. Principle: the hour hand moves half a degree a minute.

quiz.prose: The last digits of the powers of 9 alternate 9, 1.
quiz.question: What is the last digit of $9^{2027}$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. An odd power of 9 ends in 9.

byKey.one: Even powers end in 1. 2027 is odd.

explain.text: The cycle 9, 1 has length 2, and 2027 is odd. So $9^{2027}$ ends in 9. Principle: reduce the power by the cycle length.

byKey.once: 16 counts each multiple of 5 once. 25, 50 and 75 bring a second 5.

explain.text: $\lfloor 80/5 \rfloor + \lfloor 80/25 \rfloor = 16 + 3 = 19$. Each 5 meets a spare 2. Principle: count factors, layer by layer.
